mappings.note: Explains why the post-Maurya centuries are called an age of reorganisation - the empire fragmenting into competing kingdoms. A period characterisation, so the goal rather than LO-101, which needs a specific administrative or military measure.
A note on Sangam literature, its dates, patrons and the Madurai assemblies - a body of source material for South Indian history. Squarely the goal's 'types of sources' clause.

Satavahana kings using their mother's name, read as evidence of the standing of royal women. Social history from inscriptions; C-SST4.1's outcome on disadvantages faced by women belongs to the civics goal and to the present day.
An open note on any kingdom of the chapter with reasons for the choice. Too broad for a single LO, so the period-history goal is the honest fit.

Inventing a kingdom with an emblem, a royal title, values, rules and taxation is an exercise in how a state is constituted and governed. Not CG-SST2, because the content is administration rather than a historical development.
Marking the chapter's ancient structures on an outline map places monuments in historical geography. Not LO-103, because nothing about their style or construction is asked.
Defines the 'Age of Reorganisation' as regions restructured into new kingdoms. Period characterisation under the goal.
Pushyamitra Shunga killing the last Maurya - dynastic chronology. Not LO-101, since no measure of rule is examined.

The northwest exposed to invasion once central Mauryan control collapsed is about the loss of military and administrative control over a frontier. Not CG-SST2, because the item reasons about control rather than narrating events.
A matrimonial alliance as a strategic instrument between royal houses is a device of statecraft and diplomacy. Not CG-SST2, because it is about how kingdoms secured themselves.
The ashvamedha performed to assert sovereignty over neighbours is a political claim to imperial standing. Not LO-104: the yajna is an old Vedic rite used for power, not a new religious idea.

The Shunga revival of Vedic ritual read as renewed emphasis on older traditions alongside surviving Buddhism. Not LO-104, which asks what led to new religious ideas, whereas this is a return to established ones.
Patanjali and the Yoga Sutras dated to the Shunga period - intellectual history and a text of the age. Not LO-104, because no movement's emergence is analysed.

The carved railings and narrative reliefs added to the Bharhut Stupa are a development in religious architecture and its decoration, which is what LO-103 covers. The frame names temples, tombs and mosques; a stupa is the nearest of those in this period.
Compares the Satavahana and Mauryan realms by size and region - historical geography. Not LO-102, because territory rather than the rulers' policies is compared.
Matches Satavahana rulers to their characteristics, keyed on Gautamiputra's matronymic. Dynastic and social recall under the goal.
Ships on Satavahana coins inferred as evidence of maritime trade - reading a numismatic source. The goal's sources clause, not an administrative measure.
The Naneghat caves used to collect tolls on a trade route is revenue administration. Not CG-SST2, because the question asks what the state did there.

A queen's grants of land, cattle and coin to priests and monks read as royal patronage - a policy of the ruling house. Not LO-104, because supporting existing institutions is not the emergence of a new religious idea.
Accepts the matronymic and rejects the claim that women had no influence, citing Gautami Balashri's inscriptions. Social history read from sources, not a civics equality outcome.
Matches sites to the dynasties that developed them and rejects Naneghat as Kushana. Historical geography and period placement rather than architecture proper, so not LO-103.
Statements on the Satavahanas' Deccan realm, Roman trade and their support for Buddhist and Jain institutions as well as Vedic rites. Broad period history.

Defines rock-cut architecture as carving directly out of living rock - a construction technique, which is LO-103's technology clause. Not CG-SST2, because the item is about how such monuments were made.
The Hathigumpha inscription written in Brahmi - identifying the script of a key source. The goal's sources clause; LO-101 would fit an item about what Kharavela actually did.

Kharavela's claim to respect every sect and repair every temple is a ruler's declared policy towards religious communities. Not LO-104, because no new movement is arising - an existing ethos of patronage is being asserted.
Identifies Sangam literature from its akam and puram themes. A source-identification item under the goal.
The Silappadikaram moving through Chola, Pandya and Chera lands - literature as a window on the three Tamil kingdoms. Not LO-101, since no governance is involved.
Attributes the Kallanai to Karikala Chola. A recall of who built it; the item stops short of analysing irrigation as an administrative measure, which would have made it LO-101.
'Keralaputra' as an epithet for the Cheras - dynastic and regional naming. Not LO-101.
Chera spices and timber against Pandya pearls - the trading profile of two kingdoms. Not LO-102, because what is compared is their exports, not the policies of their rulers.
Places the Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas and Satavahanas in order and origin. Chronology and provenance under the goal.

The Heliodorus pillar as an instance of cultural interaction and assimilation - a Greek envoy adopting Indian devotion. Not LO-104, because the item names the process of blending rather than analysing a religion's emergence.
The 78-year offset of the Shaka Samvat is chronology and calendar history. No LO covers dating systems.

Gandhara art as a fusion of Indian Buddhist themes with Greco-Roman technique. Not LO-103, whose scope is the construction of temples, tombs and mosques; Gandhara sculpture is imagery, not a building.
Grey-black schist against red sandstone as the materials of two sculpture schools. Art history; LO-103 would apply to building technique, not to the stone of statues.
Kanishka and Kushana control of stretches of the Silk Route - trade and connectivity. Not LO-101, because the item names the route rather than a measure of control.
Identifies a school of art from anatomy, drapery and stone - reading a sculptural source. Not LO-103, since no building is involved.
Matches dynasties to the regions they ruled and rejects the Cheras in Kalinga. Historical geography under the goal.

Invading groups adopting Indian religions, art and customs as the explanation of their assimilation. A cultural-development judgement; LO-104 would need a new religious movement to be arising, not existing ones being adopted.
Statements on Sangam literature's language, Karikala and the Grand Anicut, and Pandya pearl fisheries. Mixed period recall, so the goal.
